clue.text: Witch, upset about one scheme being rejected, casting spells

definitions.note: a gerund phrase naming the activity; the answer is a noun for that activity

indicators.note: something upset is knocked into disorder, so the letters of the first word get jumbled
a thing rejected is sent back, so the words for one scheme are read backwards
about means surrounding here, so the jumbled letters wrap round the other piece

blocks.note: taken as written, as the anagram fodder
one is the Roman numeral I
a game is a scheme or plan, as in 'what's your game?'

explanation.surface: A witch, annoyed that one of her plots has been turned down, takes to casting spells.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Witch' looks like the definition, but it is only the fodder; the definition is the activity at the far end of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: White magic is sorcery used for good ends, which in practice means working charms and incantations.

clue.text: Chicken crossing a road that's concrete

definitions.note: used as a verb, to set solid

indicators.note: a thing crossing a road spans it, so the bird's word stretches across, enclosing the other

blocks.note: a hen is a female chicken
taken as written
RD is the abbreviation for road

explanation.surface: The old joke of a chicken crossing the road, here a tarmac or concrete one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concrete' reads as a noun or adjective, but it is the verb meaning to set solid.
explanation.definitionFit: To concrete can mean to solidify or make firm, which is what hardening does to a material.

clue.text: Combined to irritate the lady

blocks.note: to get at someone, or simply 'it gets me', means to annoy: to get
her refers to a woman

explanation.surface: Two aims rolled into one: annoying a particular woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Things done together are joined or united in one effort, which is what combined describes.

clue.text: What determines tournament champion, possibly

blocks.note: surface reading: whatever decides who wins a competition overall
setter's reading: in tennis, the final point of the final can decide the title, though it may not

explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' is fair because the moment only decides the championship if it is converted in the final.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis this is the rally which, if won, ends the match, and in the final it settles who takes the trophy.

clue.text: Part of boat in which fish can be heard

indicators.note: something heard is taken by sound, so the spoken form of the fish matters, not its spelling

blocks.note: the gunnel is a small eel-like fish of northern shores

explanation.surface: A part of a boat where you can hear fish.
explanation.walkthrough: Sailors say this word 'gunnel', exactly like the name of the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The gunwale is the top edge of a boat's side, once where guns were mounted.

clue.text: Players project style

blocks.note: first meaning: the actors in a play or film
second meaning: to throw or direct, as a shadow or a glance
third meaning: form or quality

explanation.surface: A group of performers puts on a stylish production.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means the company of actors, to throw or direct something, and a characteristic form or turn of mind.

clue.text: Tune's tempo establishes the atmosphere

blocks.note: an air is a tune, with the possessive 's
tempo is speed, or pace

explanation.surface: A melody's speed sets the mood of a piece of music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'atmosphere' looks like mood, the musical sense the surface wants; here it means the sky above.
explanation.definitionFit: Airspace is the region of sky above a country, part of the layer of gases surrounding the earth.

clue.text: Fighting in the underground

blocks.note: first meaning: the act of opposing or fighting back
second meaning: a secret movement opposing an occupying power, like the French one in the Second World War

explanation.surface: A scuffle breaks out on a Tube train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the underground' suggests London's Tube railway; it is the clandestine opposition movement.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means opposition by force, and also names the covert organisations that fought occupiers in wartime Europe.

clue.text: Do I have a voice?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone asking whether they get a say
setter's reading: the grammatical voice, where a subject like 'I' doing something is the opposite of passive

explanation.walkthrough: The sentence 'Do I...' has the subject performing the action, so the voice it is written in is the grammatical one where the subject acts.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammar names two voices for verbs; the one where the subject performs the action carries this name, opposite to passive.

clue.text: Cow is straight into the marshy area

indicators.note: one thing put into another sits inside it, so the word for straight goes within the marsh

blocks.note: right as in a right line or angle, meaning straight
a fen is low marshy land, as in the East Anglian Fens

explanation.surface: A cow wanders straight into a bog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cow' looks like the animal, but it is the verb meaning to intimidate.
explanation.definitionFit: To cow someone is to scare them into submission, so the verb for making afraid substitutes neatly.

clue.text: Risk a wet fall

indicators.note: a fall tumbles things out of place, so the preceding letters come down in a new order

blocks.note: the eight letters taken as written, as the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A warning that you may end up soaked if you tumble.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the fodder with its signal and a description: skimming behind a boat, you chance a soaking tumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Gliding over a lake on skis towed by a boat carries an obvious danger of plunging into the water.

clue.text: Heads off into Northern Canada, hoping to locate a small island

indicators.note: the heads of words are their leading letters, so only the opening letter of each is kept

blocks.note: the initial letters of these four words

explanation.surface: Travellers set off into the Canadian north in search of a tiny island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' is part of the surface journey; the signal is just 'Heads'. Inch is a Scottish word, as in Inchcolm in the Firth of Forth.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scotland, inch (from Gaelic innis) names a small island, a sense mostly met in place names and crosswords.

clue.text: I slip up, with the result that cement is not firm

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, so the word runs backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
to err is to make a slip
so means with the result that, as in 'it rained, so we stayed in'
lute is a clay or cement used to seal joints

explanation.surface: A builder admits a mistake, and the cement has not set.
explanation.walkthrough: ERR goes up to read RRE, giving I + RRE + SO + LUTE.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone irresolute is wavering and undecided, lacking firmness of purpose.

clue.text: It's very different, with Europeans out of consideration

definitions.note: the clue reads 'It's very different', an adjective phrase like the answer

blocks.note: people from Poland
as in 'joking apart', set aside and not considered

explanation.surface: Something quite unlike the rest, since the Europeans have been left out of the reckoning.
explanation.definitionFit: Two things at opposite ends of the earth are as far apart as can be, hence the idiom for utterly unlike.

clue.text: Dish removed from the menu after a strong representation

indicators.note: a representation shows something in another form, so these letters are presented in a different order
after sets the piece meaning taken off the menu behind the jumbled letters, reversing the clue's order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written, as the anagram fodder
a dish that is off is no longer available

explanation.surface: A dish is struck off the menu after a firm complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' places the second piece behind the first, as the order of the answer requires.
explanation.definitionFit: Beef stroganoff is a Russian dish of strips of meat cooked in a sour cream sauce.

clue.text: Burden official with bucket

blocks.note: short for referee, the official at a match
to bucket down is to pour with rain

explanation.surface: Someone loads an official with a pail to carry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Burden' looks like a verb about loading, but it is the old noun for the chorus of a song.
explanation.definitionFit: Burden in its musical sense is the recurring chorus of a song, the lines repeated after each verse.

clue.text: Struggle with fish

blocks.note: first meaning: to thrash about clumsily or be in difficulty
second meaning: a flatfish

explanation.surface: An angler battles with a catch on the line.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to stagger or struggle helplessly, and the noun is a flatfish related to the plaice.

clue.text: Part exchange iodine for oxygen in exploit

indicators.note: 'X for Y' means X takes the place of Y, so one element is swapped for the other

blocks.note: I is the chemical symbol for iodine
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen
to trade on something is to exploit it

explanation.surface: A chemistry lab sounds as if it is swapping one element for another in a reaction.
explanation.walkthrough: TRADE ON with its O replaced by I gives TRADE IN. Part exchange is the British term for handing over an old item as partial payment.
explanation.definitionFit: Part exchange means giving an old car or device as part payment for a new one, which is a trade-in.

clue.text: Kill spymaster -- always boss

blocks.note: to do in is to kill
M is the head of the secret service in the James Bond stories
e'er is a poetic contraction of ever

explanation.surface: An order to assassinate a spy chief, from a boss who always gives orders.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter gives no signal that the spymaster goes inside the word for kill; the solver has to see it. E'ER is poetic shorthand for ever.
explanation.definitionFit: To domineer is to rule over people arrogantly, to boss them about.

clue.text: Superior stovepipe?

blocks.note: first meaning: snobbish, haughty
second meaning, hinted by the question mark: a tall hat like Abraham Lincoln's

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that a stovepipe hat is only one example of a tall hat.
explanation.definitionFit: High-hat is slang for snooty or condescending, and literally a tall hat, of which a stovepipe is an example.

clue.text: Used to tie up the petty cash

definitions.note: a phrase for a tiny sum; the answer means a very small budget

blocks.note: first meaning: the lace that fastens footwear
second meaning: a meagre amount of money, as in running things on a tight budget

explanation.surface: Someone ties up the petty cash, perhaps bundling notes with string.
explanation.definitionFit: A lace fastens footwear, and doing something on a small budget is idiomatically doing it on this cheap cord.

clue.text: Sir Thomas and Sir John losing heart

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letter, and losing it means that letter is dropped

blocks.note: Sir John Moore, the general killed at Corunna in 1809

explanation.surface: Two famous knights, one of them losing his nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: MOORE minus its middle O gives MORE.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Thomas More was Henry VIII's Lord Chancellor, author of Utopia, executed in 1535 and later canonised.

clue.text: About to sit and take a rest

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
to sit for a portrait is to pose

explanation.surface: Someone is about to sit down and have a breather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to' reads as 'on the point of', but 'About' is one piece and 'to sit' another.
explanation.definitionFit: To repose is to lie down or relax, which is taking a break from activity.

clue.text: Many with mental suffering become depressed

blocks.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, a crossword stand-in for many
anguish is severe mental pain

explanation.surface: Large numbers of people in mental distress sink into depression.
explanation.definitionFit: To languish is to lose vigour and pine away, growing weak and dispirited through neglect or sorrow.

clue.text: Knowledgeable about contents of print-out

indicators.note: the contents of something are what lies inside it, so the letters sit within the following word

blocks.note: the letters run inside this word, across its hyphen

explanation.surface: Someone who understands what a computer print-out says.
explanation.definitionFit: Being into a subject, informally, means being keen on it and well versed in it.

clue.text: The way in which goose is mistaken for a pen

indicators.note: a word that is mistaken is got wrong, so its letters come out in the wrong order
something placed in which another sits is the outer piece, so one goes inside the other

blocks.note: how means the way in which something is done
taken as written, as the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Someone describes how a goose gets confused with a pen, the farmyard kind or the writing kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pen' is not the writing tool or the enclosure for a goose; it is slang for prison, short for penitentiary.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoosegow is American slang for a jail, from Spanish juzgado, so it names the same place as a pen.

clue.text: Prime mover in the robbery, he believes

definitions.note: a clause describing the person; the answer is a noun naming him

indicators.note: the prime, or first, mover in a word is its leading letter, which alone is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of this word
a heist is a robbery

explanation.surface: The ringleader of a robbery claims to be a believer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prime mover' suggests God or a gang boss; here it only means the first letter of 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: A theist is someone who holds that a god exists, so he is defined as one who believes.

clue.text: Ex-monk is not working

definitions.note: a verb phrase; the answer is an adjective phrase that follows 'is'

blocks.note: first meaning, read cryptically: a former monk has left his religious order
second meaning: broken, as on a sign hung on a faulty machine

explanation.surface: A man who has left the monastery is now unemployed.
explanation.definitionFit: Monks belong to religious orders, so one who has left is cryptically outside his; a broken machine carries the same notice.
